paras: The White Hall sawmill whitecapping was the expulsion of Black laborers from the Davis and Hodges sawmill at White Hall, Poinsett County, Arkansas, by a band of eleven white men on August 17, 1903. The men were arrested by a federal deputy marshal, and in March 1904 three of fifteen defendants were convicted in federal court at Helena and sentenced, two of them to the penitentiary. The Cleveland Gazette called it the first time white men in that section had been convicted in federal court of whitecapping Black people, and the defense appealed to the United States Supreme Court.

The mill, owned by Davis and Hodges, was 'operated exclusively by negro labor' in a community that a Wynne correspondent described as 'thickly populated with negroes.' Federal authorities were also pursuing white men in neighboring Cross County for driving Black residents out, and some reports grouped the cases together.

About 10 o'clock on the morning of August 17, eleven white men, most of them 'well to do planters' and one a school teacher, went to the mill in a body and unmasked. They ordered the Black workers out, threatening them with violence if they did not leave at once, and the workers complied. The mill shut down, and the owners were forced to suspend business temporarily.

On August 21 Deputy United States Marshal U. G. Copeland brought the eleven men, whom the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic named, through Wynne to Helena for a hearing before a federal commissioner. According to the wire report, the arrests were made at the mill owner's instigation.

The eleven were bound over to the October federal grand jury at Helena under $1,000 bonds. On October 8, 1903, that grand jury indicted twenty-seven white men for intimidating Black people: twelve from Cross County, and the rest from Poinsett, charged with forcing Black workers to leave the sawmill through threats. The charge was conspiracy, and in January 1904 Judge Jacob Trieber refused to reduce bonds for seven Cross and Poinsett defendants held in jail.

Fifteen Poinsett defendants were tried at Helena in March 1904, and the jury found three guilty, Reuben Hodges (printed 'Reug Hoges'), William Clampit and Wash McKinney, with a recommendation of mercy, while twelve were discharged. By the account after the verdict, the charge was that the men had threatened the workers 'with death should they fail to leave the community.' Judge Trieber passed sentence about March 19: Hodges and Clampit received a year and a day in the Atlanta penitentiary and a $100 fine each, and McKinney sixty days in the Lee county jail and a $100 fine. The defense appealed to the Supreme Court to test the federal statute enforcing the Fourteenth Amendment, arguing that it gave Black citizens a protection in federal courts 'that is not given to white men.'

A short wire datelined Wynne, August 22, ran under headlines such as 'White Capping Is Charged' and 'Whitecappers Arrested,' describing the accused as 'prominent planters'; one copy put their number at twelve. The fullest account came from a Wynne correspondent of the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, which named the men, called them 'whitecappers,' and reported the owners' view that personal enemies were behind it. The Vicksburg Herald, quoted in Hattiesburg, called whitecapping an 'abominable business' and hoped the indictments would end it. At sentencing, northern papers such as the New-York Tribune and San Francisco Call framed it as a 'Negro Rights Test Case' bound for the Supreme Court.

The Black press carried the case at both ends: the Cleveland Gazette reprinted the August wire under 'Eleven Whites Arrested by Uncle Sam,' substituting 'Afro-American' for the wire's 'negro.' After the verdict the Gazette ran 'Convicted Ringleaders,' the only report to say the attackers acted because 'white men' wanted the workers' places. The Wichita Searchlight gave the sentences under 'Whitecappers to Atlanta Pen,' and the Baltimore Afro-American noted them in one line.

Accounts of motive differ: the mill owners suspected 'some personal enemies, or grudge' against themselves, while the Cleveland Gazette said white men wanted the Black workers' jobs. The Sharp County Record called the fifteen tried 'Cross county citizens,' but other reports of the verdict place them in Poinsett County.

bases: An unmasked band of eleven white men, called 'whitecappers' and charged in federal court with conspiracy, ordered Black laborers out of a sawmill under threats, closing it (A3, A10, A16).

accounts.label: Wynne wire
accounts.gist: A band of white planters drove the Black mill hands off with threats, the mill suspended, and a deputy marshal arrested eleven planters at the mill owner's instigation.

accounts.label: Wynne correspondent (Pine Bluff Graphic)
accounts.gist: Eleven named men entered the Davis and Hodges mill unmasked on the morning of August 17 and ordered the Black workers out under threat of violence; the owners blamed personal enemies, since no other Black residents were bothered.

accounts.label: Black correspondent after the verdict (Cleveland Gazette)
accounts.gist: Fifteen prominent citizens were indicted for forcing Black men to quit work at the sawmill because white men wanted their places; three ringleaders were convicted.

framing.detail: 'White Capping Is Charged. Eleven Prominent Planters Arrested': the wire stresses the standing of the accused and the federal arrest.
The local Pine Bluff report names the accused, calls them 'whitecappers', and calls the mill owners 'highly respected gentlemen'.
The Vicksburg Herald, quoted in Hattiesburg, called whitecapping an 'abominable business' and hoped the indictments would end it.
The New-York Tribune headlined the sentencing as a 'Negro Rights Test Case' headed for the Supreme Court.
The Cleveland Gazette headlined 'Eleven Whites Arrested by Uncle Sam' and later 'Convicted Ringleaders', a first for the section.
The Wichita Searchlight ran the sentences under 'Whitecappers to Atlanta Pen' and 'Men Terrorized Negroes Are Sentenced in Arkansas'.

conflicts.note: The local report names eleven men (A3); 'twelve' appears in one copy of the wire.
Several Helena reports place the convicted men in Poinsett; the Sharp County Record brief likely conflated them with the separate Cross county cases (A12, A21).
